messages.author: 62df6b9d8121ed48
messages.subject: Hierarchical State Space Dynamics
parts:
Hello,

I'm trying to implement a hierarchical state space regression model in rstan that follows the methodology of this paper: https://ppw.kuleuven.be/okp/_pdf/Lodewyckx2011AHSSA.pdf

The basic idea is that you have N subjects through time and want to find relationship between y(t,n) and lagged values of y(,n) and  x(t,n) , where t is time,  n is subject id, y is variable of interest, and x are  The regression coefficient beta is assumed to be drawn from a multivariate normal distribution for each individual.

Since its a state space model I tried to code it in terms of "Matt's Trick" found here https://gist.github.com/jrnold/5e0fb240369311bb2f3b to be more efficient.

The code I wrote is does not sample and gets error:
Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is 1.#QNAN:0, but must be finite!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.


Any tips or observations on how to fix his error or write better code would be very much appreciated

My code and data are here: https://github.com/samcarlos/Rstan-Hierarchical-State-Space-Dynamics

Thanks in advance,
Sam

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical State Space Dynamics
parts:
When I tried running your example I got a different error message:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is nan:0, but must be finite!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
 Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.


I've been trying to strip down your model to figure out what's causing this, but no luck so far. There's definitely a couple places you could probably clean things up, e.g. inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001) is probably way too wide, I don't think you need to create y_data_observed, but can instead do something like: 

for (n in 1:N) {
    for (t in (2+L):T){
        if(!y_data_indicator_missing[t,n])
            y_data[t,n]~normal(theta[n,t] , sigma_y);
    }
}

(once you get everything working you can add back in your unobserved data the same way, or perhaps more robustly, sample it in post-processing step in R or in the generated quantities block in Stan.)

You also shouldn't need to transform sigmasq_y to sigma_y; you can just put a prior on sigma_y (see manual for examples). Does sigmasq_beta get used?

Overall, I'd suggest making your model as simple as possible, fixing all the parameters at reasonable values (you can do this by moving them to the data block and then passing in fixed values -- it's no problem to leave the sample statement in the model block, it won't do anything!) and trying to get something that at least samples, then add features of the model back in one by one until you figure out what's causing the issue.

Happy to try to figure out what's wrong with a simpler model, just send it back to the list. But do please try to indent your code for readability. ;)

HI Seth,

I cleaned up code without y_data_observed (I'll include it later but since data is complete, I'll ignore it) here: https://github.com/samcarlos/Rstan-Hierarchical-State-Space-Dynamics/blob/master/HSSD_Test_1.R.  The code gets the error:

Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.

Not sure why we're getting different errors.


I then tried to make more simple by modeling theta as a unit root process (no lagged values of theta other than (t-1) ) and this sampled fine. Because of this it seems like including lagged values of theta is causing a hiccup in sampling.  The code for this is here: https://github.com/samcarlos/Rstan-Hierarchical-State-Space-Dynamics/blob/master/HSSD_Test_1_noLaggedTheta.R .


When you say "fix all values at reasonable values", do you mean explicitly declaring something like : "sigmasq_y <- 1" as opposed to  "sigmasq_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001)"?

Thanks Again!,
Sam

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical State Space Dynamics
parts: > When you say "fix all values at reasonable values", do you mean explicitly declaring something like : "sigmasq_y <- 1" as opposed to  "sigmasq_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001)"?

You can't assign to a parameter in the model block but you could do this:
transformed data {
  real sigmasq_y;
  sigmasq_y <- 1;
}

But I think it's easier to play around with values by putting it in as data;
data {
  real sigmasq_y;
}

Because then you can leave the sampling statement in the model block (that's what I was saying about it not affecting anything) and mess around with different values passed in as stan.dat. (You'll need to remove the declaration from the parameters block.)

Maybe your issue is theta_innovation? You declare it as:
matrix[T,N] theta_innovation;

But then what does this do? Isn't the indexing off?
for(n in 1:N) theta_innovation[n]~normal(0,1);

Maybe this is what you meant?
for(t in 1:T) for(n in 1:N) theta_innovation[t,n]~normal(0,1);

Or this?
for(t in 1:T)
theta_innovation[t]~normal(0,1);

It seems to sample now! 300 iterations took 125 seconds.

Best,
Seth

On Sun, May 24, 2015 at 6:20 PM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
When I tried running your example I got a different error message:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is nan:0, but must be finite!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.


Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
 Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.


I've been trying to strip down your model to figure out what's causing this, but no luck so far. There's definitely a couple places you could probably clean things up, e.g. inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001) is probably way too wide, I don't think you need to create y_data_observed, but can instead do something like: 

for (n in 1:N) {
    for (t in (2+L):T){
        if(!y_data_indicator_missing[t,n])
            y_data[t,n]~normal(theta[n,t] , sigma_y);
    }
}

(once you get everything working you can add back in your unobserved data the same way, or perhaps more robustly, sample it in post-processing step in R or in the generated quantities block in Stan.)

You also shouldn't need to transform sigmasq_y to sigma_y; you can just put a prior on sigma_y (see manual for examples). Does sigmasq_beta get used?

Happy to try to figure out what's wrong with a simpler model, just send it back to the list. But do please try to indent your code for readability. ;)

Hey Seth,

That code doesn't include the "lagged_thetas" variable. It assumes a unit root process not include:


for(n in 1:N)
for(t in (1+L):T)
for(l in 1:(L-1))
lagged_theta[n,t]<-beta[n,P*L+l]*theta[n,t-l] + lagged_theta[n,t];

I'll play around with it to see if I can get rid of that lagged_theta variable. 

Thanks,
Sam

data {

}

matrix[T,N] theta_innovation;

But then what does this do? Isn't the indexing off?
for(n in 1:N) theta_innovation[n]~normal(0,1);

Maybe this is what you meant?
for(t in 1:T) for(n in 1:N) theta_innovation[t,n]~normal(0,1);

Or this?
for(t in 1:T)
theta_innovation[t]~normal(0,1);

It seems to sample now! 300 iterations took 125 seconds.

Best,
Seth

instead of :
 for(n in 1:N) beta[n]~multi_normal(mu_beta,Sigma_beta);

 for(n in 1:N) for(p in 1:num_vars) beta[n,p]~normal(mu_beta[p],Sigma_beta_vetcor[p]);

The posterior distribution will still have correlated beta distribution, but it won't be explicit in the prior. 

Thanks again,
Sam

> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:

> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,

> I've been trying to strip down your model to figure out what's causing this, but no luck so far. There's definitely a couple places you could probably clean things up, e.g. inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001) is probably way too wide, I don't think you need to create y_data_observed, but can instead do something like:
>
> for (n in 1:N) {
> for (t in (2+L):T){
> if(!y_data_indicator_missing[t,n])
> y_data[t,n]~normal(theta[n,t] , sigma_y);
> }
> }
>
> (once you get everything working you can add back in your unobserved data the same way, or perhaps more robustly, sample it in post-processing step in R or in the generated quantities block in Stan.)
>
> You also shouldn't need to transform sigmasq_y to sigma_y; you can just put a prior on sigma_y (see manual for examples). Does sigmasq_beta get used?
>
> Overall, I'd suggest making your model as simple as possible, fixing all the parameters at reasonable values (you can do this by moving them to the data block and then passing in fixed values -- it's no problem to leave the sample statement in the model block, it won't do anything!) and trying to get something that at least samples, then add features of the model back in one by one until you figure out what's causing the issue.
>
> Happy to try to figure out what's wrong with a simpler model, just send it back to the list. But do please try to indent your code for readability. ;)
>
